newsitem.title: USA: Suspected ex-Nazi guard in U.S. may not be tried.
newsitem.headline: Suspected ex-Nazi guard in U.S. may not be tried.

text.p: A suspected former Nazi concentration camp guard alleged to have committed wartime atrocities may never be deported from the United States due to a serious medical condition, U.S. officials said on Wednesday.
Michael Kolnhofer, a 79-year-old resident of Kansas City, Kansas, was still in critical condition and on life support systems at the University of Kansas Medical Centre, a spokeswoman there said.

Chris Watney, a spokeswoman with the U.S. Attorney's Office in Wichita, Kan., said the U.S. Government would have to drop its effort to deport Kolnhofer from the United States to Croatia, where he was born, if his medical condition did not improve.

Although Kolnhofer does not face any criminal charges in the United States for his alleged wartime activity, the U.S. Department of Justice has filed a civil complaint accusing him of taking part in wartime atrocities while serving as an SS guard at concentration camps in wartime Germany.

The complaint, filed in U.S. District Court in Kansas City, alleged Kolnhofer joined the German Waffen-SS in September 1942 and served as a guard at the Sachenhausen concentration camp near Berlin until January 1944.

Kolnhofer was taken to hospital on Dec. 31 after police shot him outside his home. A bullet passed through both of Kolnhofer's legs and fractured the femur in one leg, and doctors said he may have suffered brain damage due to lack of blood pressure during surgery.

Kolnhofer had fired at police and journalists first in a confrontation that began last week after the Justice Department said it was seeking to revoke his U.S. citizenship because of alleged war crimes.

The Justice Department's Nazi-hunting Office of Special Investigations said Kolnhofer had concealed his identity when he emigrated to the United States in 1952. At the time, Kolnhofer said he had served in the German army on the Russian front.

Kolnhofer was born in Croatia when it was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. A spokesman for the U.S. Department of Justice in Washington said if Kolnhofer were to be deported, the United States would ask Croatia to take him.

After last week's shooting, local authorities also charged Kolnhofer with three counts of aggravated assault on a law enforcement officer. But a spokesman for the District Attorney in Wyandotte County, Kan., said Kolnhofer may never stand trial for these criminal charges because of his condition.
